theme: The king rejoices in your strength
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 21. It is the companion to Psalm 20. There the people prayed for the king before battle, and here they give thanks for his victory.
settingTheScene: Psalm 21 is a royal psalm of thanksgiving, likely used at a celebration of the king’s accession or a victory. Psalms 20 and 21 should be read together, as a prayer followed by a praise. The king is a figure of joy in God’s strength, and the psalm points beyond David to a king whose reign has no end.
observation: “O LORD, in your strength the king rejoices, and in your salvation how greatly he exults!” (v. 1).
“You have given him his heart’s desire and have not withheld the request of his lips” (v. 2).
“For you meet him with rich blessings; you set a crown of fine gold upon his head” (v. 3).
“He asked life of you; you gave it to him, length of days forever and ever” (v. 4).
“His glory is great through your salvation; splendor and majesty you bestow on him” (v. 5).
“For you make him most blessed forever; you make him glad with the joy of your presence” (v. 6).
“For the king trusts in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he shall not be moved” (v. 7).
“Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! We will sing and praise your power” (v. 13).
interpretation:
Where Psalm 20 asked, Psalm 21 gives thanks. The pattern is a reminder that prayer is not only petition. Many of us ask and forget to thank. The people here return to God to say that he has answered. The king’s heart’s desire has been given. The language is of overflowing generosity: rich blessings, a crown of gold, glory, splendor, majesty.

A phrase in verse 4 is striking: “He asked life of you; you gave it to him, length of days forever and ever.” In terms of the historical David, “forever” might be read as a long life, or as the length of his dynasty. But “forever and ever” reaches further. It points to a king who will live and reign eternally. Psalm 21 asks us to read it with more than David in mind.

The root of the king’s blessing is stated at the end: “For the king trusts in the LORD.” His strength is not his own. The word “trusts” is the key to his success. He will not be moved, “through the steadfast love of the Most High.” The king’s security rests on God’s covenant love.

Verses 8 to 12 describe judgment on the king’s enemies. The imagery is strong: a fiery furnace, a consuming fire. These lines are not an invitation to violence, but a recognition that the reign of the LORD’s anointed brings the end of all who oppose him. It is a theme that runs from Psalm 2 to Revelation.

The psalm closes with a collective song. The people return their gaze from the king to the LORD: “Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength!” The king is blessed, but the center is always God.
connection: Hebrews 5:7-9 speaks of Christ who asked for deliverance from death and was heard. “Length of days forever and ever” is fulfilled in his resurrection (Acts 2:24-28; Revelation 1:18). “The joy of your presence” echoes Acts 2:28 and Hebrews 12:2. The crown of gold points to Revelation 14:14, where the Son of Man wears a golden crown. Philippians 2:9-11 says God has highly exalted him.
application:
Make a list of ways God has answered prayer in the last month, and thank him for each.

Ask what it means to rejoice in his strength rather than your own.

Give thanks for the King who lives forever.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for answered prayer and good gifts.
Thank Jesus, who asked for life and was given it forever.
Ask him to be exalted in his strength in your life.
